newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina to test local market with two-year bond.
newsitem.headline: Argentina to test local market with two-year bond.

text.p: Argentina Tuesday will auction its first treasury bond, or Bonte, locally this year in what will be an important guage of the demand for government debt in Argentina, financial analysts said.
If warmly received, the $500 million two-year Bonte issue will pave the way for the government to increasingly shift its debt paper financing to local rather than foreign markets, they said.
The government is eager to boost the importance of the local market as a funding source since most outstanding Argentine government bonds have been placed abroad, largely in the form of Brady bonds.
A strong market response to Tuesday's Bonte issue is seen as being the first step to issuing debt with longer maturities next year in the local market.
"A well received auction of the two-year Bontes will open the possibility of offering new Bontes with maturities of up to five years," said Fundacion Capital, a local consultancy.
The government first tested the waters of the local maket for debt paper by issuing treasury bills, or Letes, with maturities of three-, six- and 12-months.

The plan was to start with short maturities and lengthen them from three months to two years. The idea is to delineate a local yield curve, said Carlos Weitz, director of debt negotiations at the Economy Ministry.
The government is planning to issue around $3.5 billion in the local market next year, he said.
Economic Ministry officials say Tuesday's Bonte auction marks the first time in Argentina that a bond with a fixed coupon will be offered through auction with all its principal payable at maturity.
Traders and analysts surveyed by Reuters estimated the yield on the two-year Bonte will come in between a low of 7.75 percent and a high of 8.50 percent.

The last dollar-denominated treasury bill auctioned, in November, was a 182-day bill, which had a yield of 7.27 percent. The last and only one-year bill sold since the monthly Letes auctions started in July was placed at a yield of 7.35 percent.
"There is very high liquidity in the market right now and the government wants to take advantage of that," said Roberto Costa Bourdieu, senior fixed income analyst at Banco Ro.

Costa Bourdieu pointed out that the issue is still relatively small, something that could prevent it from taking off as a major local instrument. However, others say if the issue goes well it could be enlarged by auctioning another $500 million in January or February.

One distinct advantage of the Bontes is that their structure with fixed coupons are very similar to U.S. treasury bills, something that will make them easier to understand for foreign investors, argues Costa Bourdieu.

By issuing treasury bonds "the domestic market is continuing to gain in importance as a source of financing for the government," consultants Fundacion Capital added in an investor note on the auction.

Although its total debt locally is still a small portion of the total, the government's intention is clearly to gradually reduce the dependence on the international markets with Letes and Bontes," it added.
